idiom_name: async/await over the runtime's I/O completion loop (Task-based Socket/Stream APIs)
implementation_notes: The .NET runtime owns the loop: socket operations are completion-oriented (ReceiveAsync/SendAsync, SocketAsyncEventArgs, Task-based wrappers) and complete on the thread pool, so the reactor's selector, dispatch table and handler registry are never written - async/await is the idiom that replaces the classic structure. The readiness primitive that would allow the classic form exists only as Socket.Select(checkRead, checkWrite, checkError, timeout), a blocking list-based select with no scalability story, and it is justified only for interop with raw descriptors or when a handler must stay pinned to one thread. Modern .NET deliberately prefers the completion-based model, so reach for async/await plus bounded concurrency rather than a hand-written Select loop.
pitfalls: Blocking on a task (.Result, .Wait(), a lock held across an await) inside a handler converts concurrency into thread-pool starvation; the .NET analogue of blocking the reactor is a sync-over-async deadlock.

There is no user-space registry to bound: one task per connection grows without limit, so admission control (SemaphoreSlim, a bounded Channel, a connection cap) replaces the ready set that the classic loop would have.

Socket.Select is the only readiness primitive and it blocks the calling thread with list-based, FD_SETSIZE-era semantics; using it for a high-connection server re-creates the worst reactor and hides a thread while doing so.
